judge_assessment.explanation: Every result the judge reports is confirmed. I re-derived all ten: 3^2-2(3)+5 = 8; the x^2-9 table cells 5.9, 5.999, 6.001, 6.1 heading to 6; the graph at x = 1 (both branches arrive at the open circle (1,2) while the filled dot sits at (1,4), so the limit is 2, g(1) = 4, removable) with the left branch x+1 confirming 2; (x^2-4)/(x^2-x-2) = (x+2)/(x+1) -> 4/3; the difference-of-cubes cells 11.41, 11.9401, 12.0601, 12.61 heading to 12; the graph at x = 3 (constant branch closes with a filled dot at (3,2), falling branch opens at (3,3)), so left 2, right 3, jump, with 6-x confirming 3; the compound fraction -> -1/4; 1+a+3 = 0 giving a = -4 and then (x-1)(x-3)/(x-1) -> -2; |x-4|/(x-4) giving -1, -1, 1, 1; and p(1.9) = 4.9, p(2.1) = 5.1, limit 5. I also rendered the figure at 200 dpi and confirm it matches the key exactly, including which dots are open and which filled — the one place a graphical item usually goes wrong. The judge's visual-quality dock is likewise supported by the artifacts rather than being an impression: gate_log.txt step 13 computes 'Page budget (ws, letter): 10 problems, 88.0cm of content, ideal 4 page(s) · accepted range 2-6' and step 14 records the build at 6 pages — the sheet is 50% over its own computed ideal and passed only because the accepted band is wide. One thing beyond the judge: the Quick Answers rows for the two graph problems read '3. 2' and '6. 3', each printing only the algebraically-confirmed branch value. Problem 3 also asks for g(1) and the discontinuity type and problem 6 asks for BOTH one-sided limits, and those parts are (correctly) declared manual — but the bank gives no sign of it, so unlike a fully manual item, which prints '—', these rows look like complete single answers. Row 6's '3' is in fact only the right-hand limit.

strengths_to_preserve: The graph-reading items are verified in the only honest way: verify.json ids 3 and 6 are manual entries whose desc records the expected reading ('Expected: limit 2, g(1) = 4, removable', 'Expected: left limit 2, right limit 3, jump discontinuity'), while the algebraic confirmation the stem also demands is machine-checked as a one-sided limit with an explicit dir ('x+1' from the left -> 2; '6-x' from the right -> 3). A graph read cannot be sympified, and the packet neither pretends otherwise nor leaves the expected reading unrecorded.

The figure itself is drawn correctly at the level of detail the problems depend on: at x = 1 both branches terminate in a single open circle at (1,2) with the filled dot at (1,4) — removable — and at x = 3 the constant branch closes with a filled dot at (3,2) while the falling branch opens at (3,3) — a jump with g(3) defined. The key's note 'a jump discontinuity does not require a hole in the domain' is exactly what that construction teaches.

Problem 8 inverts the usual direction of the topic: instead of resolving a given 0/0, the student must CHOOSE a so the form becomes 0/0, and the key states the reasoning that makes it more than a trick — 'A quotient with a nonzero numerator over 0 blows up, so a finite limit forces the numerator to vanish at 1 as well', with the check that any other a sends the one-sided limits to +inf and -inf.

Each of the three evidence types is given its epistemic status in the directions and then held to it in the key: 'A table suggests a limit; it never proves one', reinforced at problem 5 ('the table says about 12, the algebra says exactly 12') and at problem 2 ('the table never reaches 6 — and it does not have to').

Problem 10's manual grading note demands the synthesis rather than the answer: 'the table suggests 5, the algebra proves it, and the sketch shows why the function still fails to be continuous until p(2) is defined to be that number. Any two of the three without the third is a partial answer.'
final_response.md's verification paragraph is accurate: 24 machine checks and four manual items, which matches verify.json exactly (ids 3, 6, 9, 10) and matches the gate log's 24 PASS lines.

root_causes.description: The Quick Answers bank renders only entries carrying an 'expected', so on a problem that mixes machine-checked and manual parts it prints the machine part alone with no label and no manual marker. Rows 3 and 6 therefore show one bare number for items that ask for three and two answers respectively, and there is no way for a grader to see from the bank that hand-reading is required — the distinction the '—' glyph exists to convey is lost precisely on the mixed rows.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 3 asks for lim g(x), g(1) and the kind of discontinuity; problem 6 asks for BOTH one-sided limits plus an explanation.
verify.json id 3: a manual entry plus a one-sided limit (expected 2); id 6: a manual entry plus a one-sided limit (expected 3, the RIGHT-hand limit).
scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry(): manual entries contribute nothing unless they are the id's only entries, in which case the row is '---'.

root_causes.description: The page-budget gate computes an ideal page count and then accepts a band wide enough that a 50%-over build passes silently. This worksheet's content measures 88.0cm, ideal 4 pages, and it built at 6 — the top of the accepted 2-6 range — with no warning anywhere in the gate log or the final response, which is the layout inefficiency the judge saw.
evidence: gate_log.txt step 13: 'Page budget (ws, letter): 10 problems, 88.0cm of content · ideal 4 page(s) · accepted range 2-6'.
gate_log.txt step 14: '6 page(s), within the 6-page budget' — reported as a pass with no mention of the ideal.
worksheet.tex problem 1 is a one-line polynomial substitution given \problem[5cm] and lands alone on page 1 beneath the figure, leaving roughly a third of the page blank above the answer rule.
verify.json declares workspace_cm for only 6 of the 10 problems, so four problems' widths in the .tex (5, 6, 7 and 7cm) were never part of the budget computation.

improvements.title: Label the graph problems' bank rows and mark the manual parts that rows 3 and 6 hide
improvements.proposed_change: When a problem id mixes manual and machine-checked entries, render both: a label per value and an explicit manual marker, e.g. '3. limit 2 (graph read: see key); left-branch check 2' and '6. right-hand limit 3; left-hand limit and reason: see key'. At minimum append the '---' marker to any row with an unrendered manual entry so the bank distinguishes fully-verified rows, mixed rows and fully-manual rows. Take the labels from a per-entry 'slot' field rather than array position.
improvements.regression_test: Feed render_quick_answers.py curr-455's verify.json and assert row 6 both names the side ('right') and carries a manual marker; assert row 4 (a fully verified single answer) carries no marker. Today row 6 renders the bare string '3', so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: A grader can tell at a glance which rows are complete and which need the worked key — the bank's entire purpose. Prevents the specific misread available here, where '6. 3' looks like the answer to 'give both one-sided limits' but is only the right-hand one.
improvements.risk: Labelled rows are wider and will push the adaptive column count down, lengthening the key slightly; on sheets with many mixed items the bank may need a stacked two-column fallback.

improvements.title: Surface the computed ideal page count when a build overshoots it, instead of passing anything inside a wide band
improvements.proposed_change: Have scripts/page_budget.py emit a WARNING (not a failure) whenever the built page count exceeds the computed ideal by more than about 25%, naming the problems whose blocks are consuming the extra height, and have build.sh echo that warning into gate_log.txt and the final response. Also require a workspace_cm on every problem so the budget is computed from the same numbers the .tex uses — four of ten problems here declared none, so the ideal was derived from partial data.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with curr-455's verify.json and a 6-page build against the computed ideal of 4: page_budget.py must emit a warning line naming the overshoot and the largest contributing blocks. A build at 4 or 5 pages must not warn. The current implementation prints only 'within the 6-page budget', so the assertion fails before the change.
improvements.expected_impact: Turns the layout inefficiency the judge docked into a visible, actionable signal at build time rather than a silent pass. Two sheets of paper per worksheet is the recurring cost across a run of this size.
improvements.risk: A warning that fires often becomes noise, and the budget must never be allowed to compress workspace — the tool's stated purpose is that space never gives. The warning should therefore point at layout overhead (orphan problems, page breaks) rather than invite authors to shrink work areas.

case_summary: A genuinely interleaved limits set that earns 31/32: ten problems rotating graphical, numerical and symbolic evidence, each type given an explicit epistemic status in the directions and held to it in the key ('a table suggests a limit; it never proves one'), with all 24 machine checks re-derived and correct and the figure independently confirmed at 200 dpi to match the key's readings at both x = 1 (removable, g(1) = 4) and x = 3 (jump, g(3) = 2). The graph items are handled the right way — declared manual with the expected reading recorded in the desc, with the algebraic half machine-checked as a one-sided limit — and problem 8 inverts the topic by making the student choose the parameter that CREATES the 0/0. Two bounded defects: the Quick Answers rows for those two graph problems print a single unlabelled number ('3. 2', '6. 3', the latter being only the right-hand limit) with no marker for the manual parts, so mixed rows are indistinguishable from complete ones; and the sheet built at 6 pages against its own computed ideal of 4, which the gate accepted silently because the band runs 2-6 — the layout inefficiency behind the judge's only dock.
